divisions.question: Tony Zappia I have listened to all of the opposition speakers who have spoken on the Migration Amendment (Offshore Resources Activity) Bill 2013 and all I heard from each and every one of them was an attack on the unions, an attack on the minister, talk about refugee policy, which has nothing to do with this bill whatsoever, and talk about border protection. Not once did any member opposite specifically address the substance and the merits of this bill, which seeks to ensure that Australia's interests in offshore projects are indeed protected. I commend the member for Wills, who pointed that out so well and so clearly in his contribution to this debate. Coalition members would like to see the multinationals that control the resource industry in Australia, both onshore and offshore, continue to operate without any restrictions and responsibilities. It is time that that came to an end. There is no logical reason whatsoever why the resources that are found offshore should be treated differently to the resources found on land in Australia and why workers who work on those resources on land should be treated any differently to the workers who are dealing with the resources found in the oceans. This legislation arises from the Federal Court decision in the Allseas v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship case. The court found that the foreign workers in that case—those on board the two pipe-laying vessels _Lorelay_ and _Solitaire_were not within the Australian migration zone and therefore did not require Australian visas. As a result of that decision, a task force was convened. I make it clear that that was done by the previous minister for immigration, not the current minister, whom members opposite seek to condemn and criticise because of what they refer to as his self-interest in this matter. The task force was asked to consider a response to the Federal Court decision so as to ensure that those projects did in fact fall within Australian jurisdiction. I note that th

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2013-06-27.66.1) to agree with [the bill's](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5086) main idea. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill for a [second time](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). This means that the Senate can now discuss it in more detail. ### What was the bill's main idea? The [bill was introduced](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5086) *"to provide that foreign workers who participate in, or support, offshore resources activities are taken to be in the migration zone and are required to hold a visa."* Read more about the bill and its background in the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1314a/14bd010).
John Hogg The question now is that the remaining stages of this bill be agreed to and this bill be now passed.

speeches.speaker: Scott Morrison
speeches.brief: Opposed the Migration Amendment (Offshore Resources Activity) Bill 2013, arguing it is designed to appease the Maritime Union of Australia, which has donated $3 million to Labor since the 2010 election, and to overturn a May 2012 Federal Court ruling in the Allseas case that offshore pipeline workers did not need visas, and announced the coalition would seek to refer the bill to a Senate committee.

speeches.speaker: Kelvin Thomson
speeches.brief: Argued for the Migration Amendment (Offshore Resources Activity) Bill 2013, responding to the Federal Court's Allseas ruling that offshore pipeline workers were outside the migration zone, and noted up to 200 vessels service the offshore oil and gas industry, over two-thirds of them foreign-flagged, with the bill expected to commence in early 2014.

speeches.speaker: Don Randall
speeches.brief: Opposed the Migration Amendment (Offshore Resources Activity) Bill 2013, calling it a union power grab that could cost employers up to $30,000 per union right-of-entry visit to offshore rigs, questioned its border security value given 44,219 unauthorised arrivals on 723 boats since 2007, and noted only 13 complaints arose from 99 inspections of 156 facilities in 2012.

speeches.speaker: Josh Frydenberg
speeches.brief: Opposed the Migration Amendment (Offshore Resources Activity) Bill 2013, warning it threatens a resources pipeline worth more than $100 billion including the $30 billion Olympic Dam project, questioned its border security implications given more than 43,000 unauthorised arrivals under Labor, and accused the government of doing the bidding of unions, which represent only 13 per cent of the private sector workforce.

speeches.speaker: Tony Zappia
speeches.brief: Argued for the Migration Amendment (Offshore Resources Activity) Bill 2013, defending it as protecting Australian jobs and fair work conditions for offshore workers rather than restricting foreign labour, noting skilled migration already accounts for about two-thirds of Australia's migrant intake, and pointed to past cases of worker abuse on foreign-flagged vessels in Australian waters.

speeches.speaker: Adam Bandt
speeches.brief: Supported the Migration Amendment (Offshore Resources Activity) Bill 2013 as a fix for the Allseas Federal Court decision that let offshore workers escape Australian labour law, but flagged a technical loophole covering vessels like dredgers that the Greens will push to close in the Senate.

speeches.speaker: Brendan O'Connor
speeches.brief: Summing up debate on the Migration Amendment (Offshore Resources Activity) Bill 2013, argued the offshore migration provisions dating to 1982, before the exclusive economic zone existed, must be updated after the Federal Court's May 2012 Allseas decision, and announced consultation on a new visa pathway before the new requirement takes effect next year.

speeches.speaker: Michaelia Cash
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the Migration Amendment (Offshore Resources Activity) Bill 2013 was drafted by former Prime Minister Gillard and Minister O'Connor to benefit the Maritime Union of Australia, not the national interest, and that it would drive international vessels and expertise away from Australian waters. The speaker also claimed the bill was introduced without proper consultation, a regulation impact statement, or consideration of Australia's international law of the sea obligations.
